batchName: Roman Religion and Mythology (753 BC-AD 391) - Medium Batch 2

questions.question: Which people did King Numa come from?
questions.explanation: Numa was a Sabine, from a hill people north-east of Rome. Tradition credits him with Rome's first calendar and several priesthoods.
questions.sourceQuote: He was a Sabine, from a hill people living north-east of Rome.

questions.question: Which organ did a haruspex especially examine in sacrificed animals?
questions.explanation: The haruspex read the entrails, above all the liver. The art came from the Etruscans and was seen as essential but slightly foreign.
questions.sourceQuote: Another kind of specialist, the haruspex, inspected the entrails of sacrificed animals, especially the liver.

questions.question: A Roman general could invite an enemy city's god to change sides, as happened at the siege of Veii. What was this ritual called?
questions.explanation: At Veii a Roman commander promised the city's goddess Juno a new home in Rome. After Veii fell, her statue was carried to Rome.
questions.sourceQuote: A general at war might even invite the enemy's god to change sides, a ritual called *evocatio*.

questions.question: Which three gods made up what modern scholars call the Archaic Triad?
questions.explanation: In the earliest era Jupiter shared worship with Mars and Quirinus, patron of citizens in peacetime. This trio was later replaced by the Capitoline Triad.
questions.sourceQuote: In the earliest era he shared worship with Mars, god of war and farming, and Quirinus, patron of the citizens in peacetime.

questions.question: Where did the Great Mother (Magna Mater), brought to Rome in 206 BC, come from?
questions.explanation: Rome's prophecy books advised bringing her in during the desperate second war with Carthage. Her eunuch priests unsettled Romans, and citizens were forbidden to join that priesthood.
questions.sourceQuote: In 206 BC, during Rome's desperate second war against Carthage, the North African power that had invaded Italy, Rome's sacred prophecy books advised bringing in the Great Mother (*Magna Mater*), a goddess from Asia Minor.

questions.question: Who was Egeria, the legendary adviser of King Numa?
options: A nymph of springs and prophecy
questions.explanation: Legend made Egeria Numa's divine companion, and through her he dealt directly with the gods.
questions.sourceQuote: Legend says he dealt directly with the gods and took advice from Egeria, a nymph of springs and prophecy who was his divine companion.

questions.question: According to legend, which god fathered Romulus and Remus?
questions.explanation: Their usurping great-uncle had forced their mother to stay a virgin, but she became pregnant by Mars, god of war. The king ordered the babies abandoned, yet they survived.
questions.sourceQuote: Their mother had been forced by her usurping uncle to stay a virgin, but she became pregnant by Mars, the god of war.

questions.question: Why did Christianity alarm Roman officials?
options: It refused to pay temple taxes
It relied on reading animal livers
Its rejection of all other gods looked like atheism
questions.explanation: A faith that rejected every other god clashed with the expectation that everyone take part in the imperial cult. Officials saw it as atheism and dangerous superstition.
questions.sourceQuote: To Roman officials, a faith that rejected every other god looked like atheism and dangerous superstition.

questions.question: In Rome itself, through what was a living emperor honoured?
options: His genius, the divine spirit in every person
questions.explanation: A living emperor was honoured through his genius. Only after death could the Senate vote him a full god.
questions.sourceQuote: In Rome, a living emperor was honoured through his genius, the divine spirit believed to live in every person.

questions.question: The Capitoline Triad of one god and two goddesses was an unusual grouping. From which people may it have come?
questions.explanation: The Etruscans, who lived in Etruria north of Rome, worshipped a similar trio. Rome's version was Jupiter, Juno and Minerva.
questions.sourceQuote: One god with two goddesses was an unusual grouping, and it may come from the Etruscans, the powerful people of Etruria north of Rome, who worshipped a similar trio.
